cues.text: A home full of football
Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, known as Ronaldinho, was born in 1980 in Porto Alegre, Brazil.
His mother, Miguelina, was a salesperson who studied to become a nurse.
His father, João, worked at a shipyard and played football for a local club.
His big brother Roberto played for the club Grêmio, and the club gave the family a new home.
But later an injury cut Roberto’s playing career short.
Many people would feel very sad if a dream ended like that.
When a dream breaks, it is okay to feel sad. Your story can still go on.
Missing Dad
When Ronaldinho was eight years old, his father died in an accident at their new home.
Losing a parent is one of the hardest things that can happen to a child.
Many children feel sad, confused or even angry, and those feelings can come back again and again.
Light the paper stars, one for each happy memory.
Families find ways to remember.
Years later, when Ronaldinho’s own son was born in 2005, he named the baby João, after his father.
It is okay to feel sad. Talk to someone you trust, and keep remembering the people you love.
The smallest player
His football began to blossom when he was eight.
He was often the youngest and smallest player in youth matches, so people called him Ronaldinho.
In Portuguese, the ending “inho” means small, and it is also a loving, friendly word.
He played futsal and beach football, and many of his famous moves came from futsal.
At 13 he scored all 23 goals in a 23–0 win.
In 1997 he played for Brazil at the Under-17 World Championship in Egypt.
Being small or different can be a strength. Keep playing your own way.
A brother who helped
In 2002 Ronaldinho won the World Cup with Brazil.
In the quarter-final against England, his free kick from far out curled into the top corner and surprised the goalkeeper.
Behind the scenes, family helped too.
Roberto’s own playing career had ended, but he found a new way to be part of football: he has worked as Ronaldinho’s manager.
Their sister Deisi has worked as his press coordinator.
Lift the flap to see who helped.
Families can help each other. When one dream ends, you can help someone else’s dream grow.
Left out, then hurt
In 2004 Brazil’s coach rested his stars, and Ronaldinho was left out of the Copa América squad.
The next year he came back as captain and led Brazil to win the 2005 Confederations Cup.
Later came a harder time.
At Barcelona his 2007–08 season was full of injuries, and in April 2008 a muscle tear in his right leg ended it.
Barcelona sold him to AC Milan.
In his second season there, he found his best form again.
A setback is not the end of the story. Rest, ask for help and try again.
Tears of joy
Ronaldinho kept playing.
At Atlético Mineiro in Brazil he wore number 49, for the year his mother was born, and in 2013 he helped the club win its first Copa Libertadores.
In April 2015, playing for Querétaro, he scored twice away at América.
Most fans there supported América, but they stood and applauded him, and he was moved to tears.
Madrid fans had applauded him once before, in 2005.
Joy can come back after sadness. Share it with the people who helped you.
